reference.source: ISSVA classification / Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies
clinicalPearls: A life-threatening consumptive coagulopathy characterised by profound thrombocytopenia occurring within a vascular tumour, not within an ordinary infantile haemangioma
It is caused almost exclusively by kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma, which trap and activate platelets
The associated tumour is typically tense, enlarging, purpuric and warm, with disproportionate swelling and bruising
Laboratory hallmarks are severe thrombocytopenia, low fibrinogen and a markedly raised D-dimer
It is distinct from the localised intravascular coagulopathy of pure venous malformations, which produces milder platelet changes with high D-dimer
Platelet transfusion is generally avoided unless there is active bleeding or surgery, because transfused platelets are consumed and may worsen tumour swelling
First-line treatment targets the underlying tumour, commonly with sirolimus and corticosteroids
Prompt haematology and vascular anomalies specialist involvement is essential given the mortality risk
reference.pathophysiology: Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon is the severe consumptive coagulopathy that complicates certain vascular tumours, principally kaposiform haemangioendothelioma and tufted angioma. The abnormal, tortuous intratumoral vasculature traps circulating platelets, which become activated and aggregate within the lesion; this intralesional platelet destruction produces profound thrombocytopenia and secondarily consumes fibrinogen and clotting factors, generating a picture that overlaps with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The resulting bleeding tendency, combined with tumour enlargement, can be rapidly life-threatening.
additionalDifferentials: Localised intravascular coagulopathy of a venous malformation (milder, without severe thrombocytopenia)
Disseminated intravascular coagulation from sepsis or other cause
additionalInvestigations: Serial full blood counts documenting profound thrombocytopenia
Fibrinogen, D-dimer and coagulation profile to confirm consumptive coagulopathy
MRI of the causative lesion to define extent and tissue involvement
Biopsy of the tumour, with GLUT1 staining, when safe to confirm kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma
Peripheral blood film to assess for microangiopathic changes
Baseline organ function tests before systemic therapy
redFlags: Rapidly falling platelet count with an enlarging, tense vascular mass
Active bleeding, mucosal haemorrhage or intracranial bleeding
Airway, visceral or retroperitoneal involvement causing mass effect
reference.prognosis: The phenomenon carries significant mortality if untreated, but with modern therapy directed at the underlying tumour (particularly sirolimus-based regimens) the coagulopathy usually resolves; residual tumour, chronic pain and fibrotic or lymphatic sequelae may remain after the acute phase.
pitfalls: Assuming a common infantile haemangioma is the cause when the culprit is a kaposiform tumour
Routine prophylactic platelet transfusion, which feeds intralesional consumption and swelling
Confusing it with the milder localised intravascular coagulopathy of a venous malformation
Delaying tumour-directed therapy while treating the coagulopathy in isolation
references: Mulliken and Young's Vascular Anomalies: Haemangiomas and Malformations
management: Direct treatment at the underlying vascular tumour (kaposiform haemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma), with sirolimus and corticosteroids as mainstays
Support the consumptive coagulopathy with fibrinogen or cryoprecipitate and fresh frozen plasma
Avoid platelet transfusion unless there is active bleeding or planned surgery, as transfused platelets are consumed and may worsen tumour swelling
Consider embolisation or surgical resection for accessible or refractory lesions
Monitor platelet count, fibrinogen and D-dimer serially to track response
Manage acutely in a high-dependency setting with multidisciplinary vascular anomalies and haematology input
